metaData.originalTitle: Inside the world’s deepest and longest subsea road tunnel
metaData.title: Inside the world’s deepest and longest subsea road tunnel
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: A first-person journey inside Norway's Rogfast tunnel, the world's deepest and longest subsea road tunnel, detailing the engineering, blasting, and human stories behind its construction.
metaData.summary: This article offers an immersive account of visiting the Rogfast tunnel project in Norway, which will become the world's deepest (390 meters below sea level) and longest (26.7 kilometers) subsea road tunnel. The author describes the drill-and-blast method used, the constant battle against seawater ingress through grouting, the complex geology involving phyllite and gneiss, and the massive logistics including ventilation shafts on Kvitsøy island. Personal experiences — from the safety briefing and rescue chambers to witnessing a controlled explosion — bring the engineering challenges to life. The piece also touches on risks like driver monotony and environmental impacts on lobster fishing, and contrasts Norway's achievements with Elon Musk's Boring Company. Ultimately, it celebrates the audacity and possibility of grand civil engineering.

mainPoints.point: The Rogfast tunnel will be the world's longest and deepest subsea road tunnel, using drill-and-blast methods.
mainPoints.explanation: At 26.7 km long and 390 m deep, Rogfast dwarfs existing subsea tunnels. Norway relies on drill-and-blast for flexibility in varied rock, adding 5–6 meters per blast.

mainPoints.point: Water ingress is the primary risk; grouting is the key mitigation technique.
mainPoints.explanation: Engineers probe ahead for leaks and inject cement-like slurry to seal fractures. The battle against water never ends; grouting speed determines overall progress.

mainPoints.point: Geology varies significantly along the route, requiring adaptive strategies.
mainPoints.explanation: Phyllite is compact but releases toxic quartz dust; granite and gneiss are hard but fractured. Seismic surveys and rock grading (1–5) guide support choices from steel rods to concrete arches.

mainPoints.point: The project includes unique features like undersea roundabouts and ventilation shafts.
mainPoints.explanation: Two roundabouts 220 m below sea level aid traffic flow. Giant shafts on Kvitsøy bring fresh air and vent car fumes, a challenge specific to road tunnels.

mainPoints.point: The human experience is central: workers endure long shifts, safety hazards, and a unique lifestyle.
mainPoints.explanation: 12-hour shifts, 12 days on/16 off in dark, damp conditions. Rescue chambers and tracking devices ensure safety. The author's firsthand blast experience captures the visceral intensity.

keyQuotes: It's kind of a lifestyle. You have to be a little bit crazy to work underground all the time.
Every blast creates a new world.
This is the longest continuous blast on the sea. Never been done before. We can't buy a book to see how we do this.
There's not necessarily just one solution to a problem. There may be many solutions.
